reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it is presented as an official music video with production credits and lyrics focused on dancing and Vitamin D. The frames show performance, crowd dancing, water, and sailboat imagery rather than a transaction or credential request. The artist links and subscription prompt are described as ordinary music-channel promotion, with no observed offer requiring payment, private data, or financial participation.

citations.quote: Monatik - Vitamin D (Official Video)
Subscribe to the Monatik channel on YouTube:
Song: Monatik Dmitriy
Do not be bored, get Vitamin D!

opening.argument: The presentation links a simple audience action with an acquisition-style promise. Viewers are told to subscribe to the channel, while the repeated imperative says to “get Vitamin D”; the lyrics also repeatedly invite participation with “Hey you! You’re there with us! Let’s get into the dance!” This creates a low-barrier call-to-action structure in which viewers are encouraged to do something immediately in exchange for access to an appealing benefit. The production does not explain what “Vitamin D” consists of, how it is obtained, or what the subscription actually unlocks. The absence of terms, eligibility, or a verifiable delivery mechanism makes the apparent offer difficult to distinguish from promotional bait.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this an official music video does not resolve the solicitation issue. The title establishes presentation, not the nature of what viewers are being encouraged to obtain. Likewise, production credits show who made the material, but do not explain what “Vitamin D” means or what subscribing delivers. The reference argument also assumes that a subscription prompt is harmless channel promotion, although the supplied description includes multiple external social and website destinations.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted call to “get Vitamin D” is plainly part of the song lyrics, not a documented reward or acquisition flow. The subscription line is ordinary channel promotion, and nothing says that subscribing produces a product, payment, access credential, or other benefit. The dance invitation is an invitation to participate in the song’s theme, not a registration or claim instruction. These quotes therefore do not establish a promise-action transaction.

opening.argument: Several signals combine into an unusually urgent promotional pattern: the material repeatedly commands viewers to “get” something, says “I’m not tired yet,” and urges them to keep going before there is time to rest. It also directs viewers toward a subscription and lists several external destinations. The visuals reinforce a high-arousal environment of crowded dancing and intense performance, including the crowd scenes in F0012 and F0047. That combination can pressure viewers to respond impulsively while leaving the supposed benefit undefined. Even if the benefit is presented through entertainment, the lack of clear terms and the repeated urgency make the solicitation materially risky.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense treats each signal in isolation. It calls the links ordinary promotion, but does not address why viewers are repeatedly told to “get” an undefined benefit or why the material uses persistent imperatives. A polished official-video label can make a solicitation more credible; it does not itself eliminate risk. The crowd imagery is also relevant because it supplies the emotional pressure surrounding the calls to action.

citations.quote: Monatik - Vitamin D (Official Video)
Do not be bored, get Vitamin D!

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Urgent-sounding lyrics are not evidence of a financial or reward scam. The phrase “I’m not tired yet” occurs in a song whose supplied text repeatedly discusses dancing and rest, while the description identifies it as a song and names the artist. The frames show performance and dancing, not a claim page, payment request, or verification step. External links and a subscription prompt are common ways to promote an artist’s channel and do not become deceptive merely because the video is energetic.

citations.quote: Song: Monatik Dmitriy

opening.argument: The apparent entertainment framing functions as promotion: the title presents an official video, the description tells viewers to subscribe, and the repeated language tells them to “get Vitamin D.” The production credits and named artist lend authority to that message, while the party and performance imagery make the call feel socially endorsed. In this reading, music is the delivery vehicle for a vague benefit and a low-friction audience action. Because the content never defines what is being obtained or what happens after subscribing, its entertainment wrapper obscures the practical solicitation rather than disproving it.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense assumes that identifying the content as a music video settles its function. But official presentation, credits, and artist links are precisely what can make promotion persuasive. The key question is not whether dancing appears, but whether the audience is steered toward an action while being promised something vague. The subscription instruction and repeated “get Vitamin D” wording remain unexplained by the defense’s characterization as harmless entertainment.

Do not be bored, get Vitamin D!

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The entertainment framing is not merely an assumption: the supplied title explicitly calls it an “Official Video,” the description identifies a song and lists dancers, and the lyrics ask people to dance. “Get Vitamin D” is a recurring lyric in that context, not a defined product or reward. The subscription request points to the artist’s YouTube channel, and the credits identify the creative team; none of this establishes a hidden participation, payment, or claim mechanism.
